headline: FERC rejects PJM's curtailment-based large-load interconnection plan, approves data center registry
summary: On Oct. 9, 2026, FERC rejected the core of PJM's plan for connecting data centers and other large loads (accession no. 20261009-3055). The rejected Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) would have let large loads connect without matching new capacity if they accepted curtailment ahead of grid emergencies. FERC found it intruded on state authority over retail rates and appeared to discriminate against large loads, but it approved PJM's large-load definition and a registry of each facility's location, ramp schedule and capacity supply. Jefferies expects PJM capacity prices to stay higher for longer and any revival to be state-led, with Ohio and Pennsylvania the ones to watch; the ruling follows FERC's rejection about five weeks earlier of key parts of PJM's backstop procurement auction.
om_angle: The order shifts curtailment-priority decisions to the states and creates a facility-level registry of large loads, a potential new dataset. Commissioner Rosner warned that leaving curtailable loads out of the capacity auction demand curve could make the auction signal ample capacity even as the region involuntarily sheds thousands of megawatts.
research_question: How does excluding interruptible large loads from capacity-market demand curves affect procurement levels, prices and reliability outcomes, compared with requiring matched new capacity?
data_identification: Use PJM capacity auction results and the forthcoming large-load registry, alongside EIA-860/861 and FERC eLibrary filings. Treat the Oct. 9 order as an event shock to IPP equity returns (Constellation, NRG, Talen, Vistra) using CRSP/Compustat. Later, compare states that adopt curtailment rules (e.g., Ohio, Pennsylvania) with PJM states that do not, at the utility-zone level.
keywords: capacity markets; interruptible load; interconnection policy; data center electricity demand; federal-state jurisdiction

headline: Utilities use collateral, deposits and longer contracts to filter speculative 'phantom' data center power requests
summary: According to a Breitbart write-up of a paywalled WSJ report (figures not verified against the WSJ text), Wood Mackenzie rates only 23% of disclosed data center power requests as high confidence. Large-customer requests to Exelon tripled to 18,000 MW. After Exelon required binding commitments and collateral, its high-probability list fell to 11,000 MW, backed by about $1 billion in posted collateral. In Texas, the connection queue exceeds 400,000 MW, large customers now pay a $50,000/MW study deposit, and minimum large-customer contract terms nationally average about 10.8 years versus about 4.6 before 2024 (per Halcyon); Vistra's CEO says demand estimates are overstated by more than 20 times.
om_angle: This is a clean setting for screening and demand-signaling under capacity investment uncertainty: collateral and contract length act as costly signals that separate serious projects from speculative ones. The figures are second-hand, so treat them as hypotheses to verify.
research_question: How much do collateral and deposit requirements reduce queue attrition and forecast error in utility large-load pipelines, and how do they shift which project types (e.g., hyperscaler vs. speculative developer) stay in the queue?
data_identification: Assemble utility rate-case and tariff filings (state PUC dockets, the source Halcyon compiled from), ERCOT large-load interconnection queue reports, and utility 10-K/earnings-call disclosures of pipeline MW. Use a staggered difference-in-differences on the timing of collateral/deposit adoption across utilities (e.g., Exelon's requirement, Texas' $50,000/MW deposit). Outcomes are pipeline MW, withdrawal rates and realized connections, measured at the utility-quarter level.
keywords: interconnection queues; demand signaling; collateral requirements; capacity investment under uncertainty; load forecasting

headline: Taylor Farms halts May–August central Mexico lettuce sourcing after a Cyclospora outbreak linked to nearly 13,000 cases
summary: In an Oct. 8 letter, Taylor Farms CEO Bruce Taylor said the company will indefinitely stop harvesting or processing central Mexico iceberg lettuce for the U.S. and Canada during the CDC's Cyclospora season (May 1–Aug. 31), which coincides with the region's rainy season. Cases linked to Taco Bell or to recalled Taylor Farms lettuce reached nearly 13,000 this summer. The FDA closed its investigation on Oct. 2 without establishing the contamination route, though it said traceback evidence pointed to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico. The company is also expanding water and crop testing, funding detection research and joining an FDA-led task force.
om_angle: This is a seasonal, risk-based sourcing exclusion rather than a full exit, a firm-level response to a food safety disruption whose root cause was never established. It raises questions about whether such responses come from learning or from signaling.
research_question: After a major outbreak, do produce buyers reallocate sourcing away from implicated regions only during high-risk seasons, and how does that affect import volumes, prices and subsequent outbreak or recall rates?
data_identification: Use bill-of-lading data (Panjiva/ImportGenius) for lettuce imports by Mexican origin region and month, USDA AMS shipment and price reports, FDA recall and outbreak records, and CDC cyclosporiasis surveillance. Apply a difference-in-differences comparing May–August with off-season months and Taylor Farms with other importers, before and after 2026.
keywords: food safety recalls; seasonal sourcing; produce supply chains; traceback; supplier region risk

headline: FreightWaves: revocation of about 25,000 Mexican drivers' B-1 visas tightens US–Mexico border trucking capacity
summary: FreightWaves reports that U.S. authorities have revoked B-1 visas for about 25,000 Mexican truck drivers; the revoking agency and the timing were not stated, and the figure is unverified. SONAR data show El Paso tender rejections peaking at about 24–25% in early July and still near 20%, San Diego/Otay Mesa at about 10% versus 3.9% a year ago, and Laredo rising from 6.07% (Oct. 3) to 7.78% (Oct. 10). Year-over-year spot rates are up 57% on San Diego–Phoenix and 43% on Laredo–Dallas. Mexico freight volumes are fairly stable, so FreightWaves attributes the pressure to lost driver supply and expects tight conditions to last well into 2027.
om_angle: A labor-supply shock to a specific mode and geography, while demand stays roughly flat, offers a rare chance to separate capacity effects from demand effects in freight markets. Canada lanes, where the issue is a freight imbalance rather than a driver shortage, offer a contrast.
research_question: How does a sudden loss of cross-border driver capacity pass through to tender rejections, spot-contract rate spreads and shippers' mode or port-of-entry substitution (e.g., rail, transloading)?
data_identification: Use lane-level tender rejection and rate data (SONAR/DAT), BTS Border Crossing and TransBorder freight data, and CBP crossing volumes. Compare Mexico border lanes with Canada border and interior lanes in an event study around the revocation timing, once the date is pinned down from DHS/State records. Shipper-level responses could be traced with bill-of-lading data.
keywords: cross-border trucking; driver supply shock; tender rejection; freight rates; nearshoring logistics

headline: Lollicup's challenge to Oregon's packaging EPR law to be paused pending NAW's Ninth Circuit appeal
summary: On Oct. 9, foodservice ware supplier Lollicup USA and Oregon DEQ director Leah Feldon jointly moved to stay Lollicup's June class action over Oregon's packaging EPR law. The stay would last until the Ninth Circuit decides the National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors' appeal, after Judge Michael Simon upheld the law in August. NAW's opening brief is due Dec. 17, and status reports would begin April 16, 2027. An Arnold & Porter partner noted that companies must still comply in the meantime, and that a Lollicup–DEQ enforcement-limiting agreement appears to have expired Aug. 31, 2026; EPR suits are also pending in California and Colorado.
om_angle: Legal uncertainty over state packaging EPR programs is a live friction for producers' compliance, fee and packaging-design decisions. The appellate timeline creates identifiable windows in which that uncertainty resolves.
research_question: Does legal uncertainty over state EPR programs delay producers' packaging redesign (material substitution, lightweighting) or registration with producer responsibility organizations, compared with states where the law is not under challenge?
data_identification: Use Oregon DEQ and the PRO (Circular Action Alliance) producer registration and fee data, state EPR program reports for Oregon, California, Colorado and Maine, and court dockets for ruling dates. Supplement with SEC 10-K risk-factor mentions of EPR and packaging-material import data from bills of lading. Run event studies around the August ruling, the Aug. 31 expiry of the enforcement agreement, and the eventual Ninth Circuit decision, at the firm-state level.
keywords: extended producer responsibility; packaging regulation; regulatory uncertainty; state environmental policy; litigation risk

headline: Designing Surprise Bags for Surplus Foods
summary: The paper studies how stores on surplus-food platforms like Too Good To Go should jointly set the reservation price and the number of surprise bags before demand and leftovers are known, given that customer ratings shape future demand. It also asks whether spreading surplus evenly across bags is actually optimal.

headline: Collective Activism
summary: The paper models whether investor collective action organizations can satisfy stewardship codes that call for coordinated activism. It finds these organizations solve free-riding among members but worsen it relative to solo activists, and that the benefit of joining is hump-shaped in the group's size.

headline: Israel's Electricity Authority moves to cap new data centers at 200 MW as grid requests reach ~27 GW
summary: Calcalist/CTech reports that Israel's Electricity Authority plans to limit any new data center to 200 MW, citing anonymous members of its governing board. A draft grid-connection decision was expected to go out for public comment. Grid operator Noga already holds connection requests from 50 facilities above 200 MW, including Mega DC (1,100 MW, Hadera) and SDS (875 MW, Nesher), which could not be approved as planned. This follows a 140-day freeze on applications of 8 MW or more, imposed after requests hit about 27,000 MW, close to three times average national load; data centers could use about 20% of Israel's electricity by 2030.
om_angle: A hard per-site size cap is a rare, clean capacity constraint on AI infrastructure. It forces firms to trade economies of scale against grid-risk concentration and may push them to split projects across sites. The case speaks directly to facility sizing, siting and interconnection-queue design.
research_question: How do per-site capacity caps change data-center project sizing, geographic dispersion and queue attrition compared with queue-based rationing such as moratoria or deposits, and what is the cost in lost scale economies?
data_identification: Build a project-level panel of Israeli connection requests from Electricity Authority decisions and public comments, Noga disclosures and press coverage. Compare requested MW, location and resubmissions before the freeze, during the freeze and after the cap, especially whether 1,100 MW proposals are re-filed as multiple ≤200 MW sites. For an analytical complement, build a stylized siting model with a size cap and a correlated-outage cost, calibrated using US large-load queue data (LBNL Queued Up, ERCOT large-load reports) as a no-cap comparison.
keywords: data center electricity demand; interconnection policy; interconnection queues; capacity caps; facility siting

headline: Australian opposition introduces bill to scrap mandatory Scope 3 reporting and drop smaller firms from climate disclosure
summary: On 14 Oct 2026, the opposition Liberal–National Coalition announced the Treasury Laws Amendment (Scrapping Scope 3) Bill 2026. Senator Jane Hume will introduce it in the Senate. The bill would remove mandatory Scope 3 reporting, which is due to start for large firms next financial year, and exempt 'Group 3' entities with $50m–$200m revenue, who join from 1 July 2027. Treasury estimates Scope 3 modelling at about $245,000 per firm in year one and about $160,000 a year after that; the Coalition puts Group 3 first-year costs at up to $70,000.
om_angle: Scope 3 mandates push emissions-data requests upstream to suppliers. Whether the mandate survives, and the uncertainty in the meantime, shapes whether firms invest in supplier data collection. As an opposition private bill, its passage is uncertain, which makes it more of a regulatory-uncertainty shock than a confirmed reversal.
research_question: Does regulatory uncertainty over a pending Scope 3 mandate cause in-scope Australian firms to delay supplier engagement and Scope 3 data collection compared with firms facing a settled mandate?
data_identification: Unit of analysis: the firm-year. Compare Australian Group 1/2 firms with matched EU/UK firms under stable disclosure regimes, using CDP supply chain responses on supplier engagement and the share of Scope 3 categories reported. Exploit the $50m revenue threshold for Group 3 in a regression-discontinuity-style comparison. Use event-study returns around the bill's announcement and any Senate votes, alongside the Clean Energy Regulator's NGER data for Scope 1 and 2.
keywords: scope 3 disclosure; mandatory climate reporting; regulatory uncertainty; supplier emissions

headline: Cyberattack on Danfoss refrigeration controllers hits ~700 French supermarkets, forcing food disposal
summary: France's finance minister said on 13 Oct 2026 that cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration systems at about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets, including stores of Coopérative U (80 of 2,000 stores, some of which discarded food), Carrefour and Monoprix. Danish supplier Danfoss said most affected systems were older products no longer receiving security updates. The Paris prosecutor's cybercrime unit is investigating losses from spoiled food and possible fires. Separately, and not linked by AP, Ahold Delhaize is restoring systems it shut down after a 'security issue.'
om_angle: This is a cyber-physical disruption in which one vendor's unsupported legacy equipment became a common-mode failure across competing retailers' cold chains. It ties together IT supplier concentration, equipment lifecycle and support policy, and perishable inventory risk.
research_question: How do the age of a retailer's installed equipment and vendor end-of-support policies affect its exposure to cyber-physical disruptions and the resulting perishable inventory losses?
data_identification: Use store-level variation within affected chains (hit vs. not hit) to estimate shrink and stockout effects, if retailer data can be obtained through partnerships. At the firm level, code cyber incidents affecting operational technology from news (GDELT, RepRisk) and industrial control system vulnerability advisories. Link these to supplier concentration measured with FactSet Revere, and test for stock-price spillovers to other customers of the same vendor using CRSP.
keywords: cyber-physical risk; cold chain; vendor end-of-support; common-mode failure; perishable inventory

headline: Rystad: battery storage is most exposed under US executive order restricting Chinese grid equipment
summary: Executive Order 14421 (26 Aug 2026) restricts foreign grid equipment that poses a national-security risk, citing AI and data-center growth. It covers transformers, inverters, battery storage, breakers, turbines and UPS batteries at critical infrastructure. Rystad finds China supplied 50% of US lithium-ion battery imports by value in the 12 months to June 2026, against 3% for transformers and under 1% for breakers; the next-largest battery suppliers are South Korea (15%) and Japan (13%). Implementing rules due by 24 Dec 2026 will define 'Covered Foreign Entity', and a broad definition could also catch Korean or Mexican plants that use Chinese components or capital.
om_angle: Because the shock varies sharply by equipment category, it is well suited to studying supplier diversification capacity and the pass-through to energy-storage deployment costs and timelines, including for data centers' backup power.
research_question: How does a sourcing restriction's impact on project costs and delays depend on prior supplier concentration, comparing batteries (50% from China) with transformers and breakers (diversified)?
data_identification: Use difference-in-differences across equipment categories, with batteries as treated and transformers and breakers as less treated. Outcomes are monthly import values and unit values by source country (USITC DataWeb, Census trade). Track storage project delays and cancellations in interconnection queues (LBNL Queued Up) and EIA-860 planned battery capacity. Timing runs from the EO signing (Aug 2026) through the definitional rule (Dec 2026) in the Federal Register. Bill-of-lading data (Panjiva) can trace transshipment through Korea and Mexico.
keywords: supplier concentration; battery storage; foreign entity of concern; sourcing restrictions; supplier diversification

headline: Mexican heavy-truck exports up 145% in September as US buyers pre-buy ahead of 2027 EPA standards
summary: Mexico exported 12,707 heavy-duty vehicles in September 2026, up 144.6% year on year, while production rose to 15,181 from 6,857 (INEGI data presented by ANPACT). Domestic retail sales fell 11.3%, the eighth straight monthly decline, and no electric or natural-gas trucks were produced or exported. ANPACT attributes the surge to US customers ordering ahead of EPA emissions standards scheduled for 2027. A 25% US truck tariff takes effect 1 Nov, and part of the jump reflects a weak September 2025 comparison.
om_angle: Pre-buying ahead of a stricter standard pulls forward fleet replacement with older-technology diesel trucks, which can delay the emissions gains the rule targets. The case links regulatory timing to capacity and production planning across a cross-border supply chain.
research_question: How large is the regulation-induced pre-buy of heavy trucks ahead of the 2027 EPA standards, and how much does the subsequent demand trough offset the rule's near-term emissions benefits?
data_identification: Run a time-series event study of monthly Mexican heavy-truck production and exports (INEGI/ANPACT) and US Class 8 imports by tariff line (USITC DataWeb). Compare these with categories not covered by the rule and with the earlier pre-buy around the 2010 EPA standards. Cross-border freight values come from BTS TransBorder. Separating the pre-buy from tariff effects is the main identification challenge, given the 1 Nov tariff date.
keywords: pre-buy behavior; fleet turnover; emissions standards; cross-border trucking; nearshoring logistics

headline: Modeling collective action in POM: The Strategy–Operations–People framework
summary: The paper imports a Strategy–Operations–People framework for collective action from organizational behavior into POM. It formalizes the framework mathematically to clarify when coordinated action, such as supply chain coordination or joint sustainability efforts, is feasible and implementable.

headline: Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
summary: Using proprietary data on Chinese corporate bond issuance, the authors find that regulators' comment letters target opaque firms and reduce issuance success. Investors connected to the issuer, however, buy more of these firms' bonds, contributing to overpricing.

headline: California finalizes SB 253 rules, setting November 10, 2026 as the first deadline for corporate GHG reports
summary: California's Office of Administrative Law approved CARB's initial corporate GHG reporting regulation on Oct. 12, 2026, effective immediately, leaving companies about a month to file. Firms with more than $1B in revenue doing business in California must report Scope 1 and 2 emissions by Nov. 10, 2026, and Scope 3 begins in 2027. In year one, CARB will accept reports without third-party assurance and lets firms use emissions data they have already collected. CARB's preliminary list puts more than 4,000 companies likely in scope. Enforcement of SB 261, the climate-risk reporting law for firms above $500M in revenue, remains paused under a Ninth Circuit injunction.
om_angle: This is a sharp, dated compliance shock with a published list of likely-covered firms, which makes it suitable for difference-in-differences designs. It also previews how Scope 3 requirements starting in 2027 will push emissions-data requests down supply chains.
research_question: Did firms newly covered by SB 253 change how they measure and report Scope 1 and 2 emissions relative to similar uncovered firms? Did their suppliers start receiving, and answering, more emissions-data requests?
data_identification: Treatment: firms on CARB's preliminary in-scope list. Controls: firms just below the $1B revenue threshold, or firms with little California activity. Outcomes: changes in CDP responses (disclosure, assurance, supply chain module requests), with EPA GHGRP facility emissions as a check on actual emissions. Supplier links can come from FactSet Revere or, as a public alternative, Compustat customer segments. Shock timing: Feb. 26 board approval, June 24 deadline extension and Oct. 12 OAL approval, which together allow an event study using SEC EDGAR filings.
keywords: mandatory climate reporting; scope 3 disclosure; supplier emissions; state environmental policy

headline: PJM to study SoftBank's ~10-GW Ohio AI campus and its gas generation and 765-kV lines under the state agreement approach
summary: PJM has filed a study agreement at FERC to evaluate SoftBank's 'Flagship' AI data center complex in Ohio, along with the generation and transmission needed to serve it, under its state agreement approach. An AEP Ohio data center tariff will serve an initial 800-MW phase. The PJM study covers another 9.6 GW of load plus 10.2 GW of new gas generation that SB Energy would build in phases through 2032. The February announcement had instead cited about $33B for 9.2 GW of gas. AEP Ohio plans three 765-kV lines, and most of the project would sit at DOE's former Portsmouth uranium enrichment site in Pike County.
om_angle: The project bundles large-load interconnection, co-located generation and policy-driven transmission planning into a single case. It raises questions of capacity sequencing and of who bears the cost of grid expansion for one customer.
research_question: How does planning large data center loads together with dedicated generation under PJM's state agreement approach change interconnection timelines and transmission cost allocation, compared with the standard interconnection queue?
data_identification: Unit of analysis: large-load and generation projects. Compare timelines, milestones and cost-allocation terms in FERC eLibrary filings for state-agreement projects with standard queue projects tracked in LBNL Queued Up data. AEP Ohio data center tariff dockets on the Ohio PUC docket system give the phased load ramp. PJM capacity auction results can show zonal price effects.
keywords: interconnection policy; data center electricity demand; interconnection queues; federal-state jurisdiction; capacity investment under uncertainty

headline: Greek draft law would require 60% renewable power for data centers, a €200k/MW grid-queue guarantee and a public registry
summary: Greece's energy ministry has drafted a law requiring data centers to source at least 60% of their electricity from renewables, met through direct connection to renewables or storage or through PPAs. Sources disagree on whether the rule covers only new sites. Developers would post a €200,000/MW bank guarantee to reserve grid capacity, could not split projects to get lighter rules, and could be offered flexible, capped connections where the grid is constrained. Grid operators would publish regional connection capacity every quarter, and the regulator RAAEY would create a data center registry. Public comment runs until Oct. 24, 2026.
om_angle: The bill combines a green procurement mandate with queue-screening collateral and capacity caps, which are policy levers OM models of siting and procurement can evaluate. If enacted, it would also generate new public data on capacity and registered facilities.
research_question: How does a per-MW collateral requirement combined with a 60% renewable sourcing mandate affect the volume of speculative data center connection requests and where data centers choose to locate?
data_identification: If the bill passes, compare connection applications and withdrawals before and after the €200k/MW guarantee, using IPTO's quarterly regional capacity publications and the RAAEY registry. Use other EU countries without such rules as a control group. Model procurement choice (PPA versus co-located storage) under the 60% target.
keywords: collateral requirements; capacity caps; facility siting; interconnection queues; data center electricity demand

headline: Circular Action Alliance cuts first-year California SB 54 EPR budget to about $1.1B in revised plan; CEO to depart
summary: Circular Action Alliance submitted a revised 495-page SB 54 packaging EPR plan to CalRecycle on Oct. 13, 2026, after a public comment period that drew more than 2,400 comments. The 2027 budget falls from up to $1.87B to about $1.11B, and the five-year range falls from $9.35B–$17.2B to $7.81B–$13.1B. The 2027 budget includes a $500M mitigation fund and a MRF capital fund capped at $100M, and the plan concedes that even PET and HDPE bottles fall short of the first plastic recycling target. CalRecycle has 75 days to act, and founding CEO Jeff Fielkow will leave later this year, with Jeff Meyers as interim CEO.
om_angle: The plan offers a rare line-item view of a PRO's cost structure, its fee-setting logic and its investments in recycling infrastructure under the largest US packaging EPR program.
research_question: How do producer fees and MRF capital allocations in SB 54's program plan relate to material-level recycling gaps? Do these fee structures create incentives for packaging redesign?
data_identification: Code the plan's budget lines and fee methodology by material from CalRecycle's SB 54 records. Compare with Oregon and Colorado PRO plans using state EPR reports, and use EPA recycling rates by material as a benchmark. Track packaging changes by covered brands over time with Mintel GNPD.
keywords: extended producer responsibility; packaging regulation; state environmental policy; litigation risk

headline: CBP proposes requiring filing by arrival for imports of $2,500 or less, plus a new postal entry type with 15-day abandonment
summary: CBP's proposed rule, published Oct. 8, 2026, would require electronic Type 11 informal entries to be filed on or before arrival, instead of within 15 days after. CBP's own sample of September–November 2025 entries found more than half would have missed that deadline. A new Entry Type 13 would cover mail shipments of $2,500 or less, with tracking numbers placed on manifests. Mail shipments not filed within 15 days would be deemed abandoned, compared with USPS's current 30-day hold. CBP says it cannot certify that the rule avoids significant impacts on small businesses, and comments are due Dec. 7, 2026.
om_angle: Tightening filing deadlines turns customs compliance into a binding operational constraint for cross-border e-commerce logistics and postal capacity.
research_question: How would moving informal entries to filing-before-arrival change clearance times, abandonment rates and the split of low-value imports between postal and express channels?
data_identification: Use the proposal's Federal Register docket and comments to gauge expected burden. Track Census trade data on low-value and postal-channel imports before and after the final rule's effective date. If accessible, Panjiva bill-of-lading data can show shifts in shipment consolidation.
keywords: regulatory uncertainty; de minimis; customs compliance; cross-border e-commerce

headline: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
summary: The paper argues that public policies often fail in implementation because they ignore operational realities. It makes the case that OM's process-level models and empirical rigor can improve how policies are designed and evaluated.

headline: NERC stakeholders approve reliability standards for data centers and crypto miners of 50 MW+ at 100 kV+
summary: NERC stakeholders passed new standards for 'computational loads' (Project 2026-02; CLO-001-1 and CLO-002-1) in a final ballot announced Oct. 15, 2026. The standards next go to the NERC Board of Trustees and then to FERC. They appear to cover loads of 50 MW or more connected at 100 kV or higher and address interconnection modeling, operational data and communications, load protection coordination and disturbance monitoring. They follow a rare Level 3 alert NERC issued in May after data centers suddenly dropped load or swung demand; NERC forecasts 224 GW of summer peak growth over 10 years, 24% above 2025.
om_angle: A hard size-and-voltage threshold creates compliance costs that may change how large loads are sized, phased and sited, and that is a natural setting for bunching designs. The standards also turn data center load behavior into a regulated operational variable.
research_question: After the standards were proposed, do new computational-load projects bunch just below 50 MW or connect below 100 kV, and does that bunching vary with how stringent the requirements are expected to be?
data_identification: Build a project-level panel of large-load interconnection requests from ERCOT large-load reports and utility or state PUC dockets, adding LBNL queue data where co-located generation appears. Compare the distribution of requested MW and voltage level before and after the May alert and the ballot, and test for excess mass just under 50 MW. Use FERC eLibrary filings to date the regulatory milestones. Applicability details were not fully verified, so check the final CLO-001-1 text.
keywords: data center electricity demand; interconnection policy; facility siting; regulatory thresholds; grid reliability standards

headline: ITC finds solar cell imports from India, Indonesia and Laos injured US makers, clearing way for AD/CVD orders
summary: On Oct. 14, 2026, the ITC voted that crystalline silicon solar cell imports from India, Indonesia and Laos injured US producers. The decision follows Commerce's final determination last month. Petitioners, led by First Solar, Hanwha Qcells USA and Mission Solar, cite India dumping margins of 123% and countervailing duty rates of 126%, and they expect final orders around Nov. 2. They also say Ethiopia has become the third-largest US solar import source, up more than 3,000% in 12 months, and have asked Commerce to investigate possible tariff evasion. A Section 232 polysilicon tariff takes effect Dec. 4.
om_angle: This is another round in a sequence of country-specific solar duties, following the 2023 Southeast Asia case. Repeated rounds let researchers trace how sourcing moves from country to country ('whack-a-mole' sourcing) and whether domestic manufacturing capacity responds.
research_question: How quickly and how completely do US solar cell imports shift to non-covered countries such as Ethiopia after successive AD/CVD actions, and does each new shift indicate transshipment, judged by the importer and supplier networks involved?
data_identification: Pull monthly HTS-level solar cell imports by country from USITC DataWeb or Census trade data. Use an event-study around the petition, the preliminary and final determinations, and the 2023 Southeast Asia case, with non-covered countries as the comparison group. For firm-level transshipment tests, use bill-of-lading data from Panjiva or ImportGenius; the public alternative is Commerce case records on exporters' ownership.
keywords: sourcing restrictions; supplier diversification; antidumping duties; tariff circumvention

headline: 836 organizations in 57 countries now commit to TNFD nature reporting as ISSB and ISO standards approach
summary: The TNFD reports that 836 organizations in 57 countries have committed to report under its recommendations, a 14% increase in under a year. They include financial institutions with more than $26 trillion in assets and listed firms worth over $10.5 trillion. More than 1,100 organizations make at least one TNFD-aligned disclosure, averaging 8 of the 14 recommended disclosures. The ISSB is about to issue a non-mandatory practice statement on nature-related disclosure, and ISO has approved turning the TNFD's LEAP approach into an ISO standard.
om_angle: The adopter list gives a ready-made sample for studying which firms choose to disclose nature-related risks. Because nature dependencies sit largely upstream, adoption may track supply chain exposure in sectors such as agriculture and mining.
research_question: Are firms with more upstream exposure to nature-intensive sectors more likely to adopt TNFD early, and does adoption change their supplier mix or sourcing disclosures afterward?
data_identification: Match the TNFD adopter list, with commitment dates, to Compustat and to supplier links from FactSet Revere; the public alternative is Compustat customer segments. Measure upstream nature exposure using the suppliers' industries. Compare early adopters, late adopters and matched non-adopters on CDP forests and water responses and on supplier changes. The ISSB and ISO milestones can serve as timing shocks.
keywords: nature-related disclosure; voluntary disclosure; biodiversity risk; scope 3 disclosure

headline: Rivian widens Redwood deal: manufacturing scrap recycling plus second-life packs powering its Illinois plant
summary: On Oct. 14, 2026, Rivian and Redwood Materials announced that Redwood will also recycle battery scrap from Rivian's manufacturing. Redwood will keep collecting used Rivian packs through Rivian's nationwide service centers; each pack is checked and either reused for stationary storage or recycled. Redwood also provides storage at Rivian's plant in Normal, Illinois, building on an April 2026 deal for a 10 MWh system made from more than 100 second-life packs to cut electricity costs and peak grid strain. Financial terms and volumes were not disclosed.
om_angle: This is a concrete case of a manufacturer combining take-back through its service network, a reuse-or-recycle grading decision, and reuse inside its own operations. Each step maps onto standard remanufacturing and closed-loop supply chain models.
research_question: For a manufacturer collecting used packs through its service network, what grading threshold and inventory policy should decide between second-life storage at its own sites and recycling, given its plant's peak electricity charges and recycled-material prices?
data_identification: Build an analytical model calibrated with public inputs: the plant's utility tariff and peak demand charges from Illinois Commerce Commission filings, storage sizing from the 10 MWh / 100+ pack figures, and recycled nickel and cobalt prices. On the empirical side, track how often firms disclose take-back and reuse in SEC filings and EIA-860 storage entries.
keywords: battery storage; second-life batteries; closed-loop supply chain; battery recycling

headline: Guardian analysis links nickel in VW, Ford and Tesla batteries to deforestation on Indigenous land in Sulawesi
summary: A Guardian analysis published Oct. 16, 2026, using company filings, two years of trade data and satellite imagery, links mines in the battery supply chains of Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla to tree loss on Tolaki Indigenous land in Sulawesi, Indonesia. Sulawesi holds the world's largest nickel deposits. According to a secondary summary, ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines moves through local smelters to Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt plants in China, and Huayou supplies cathode materials to CATL. The batteries only 'may contain' this nickel, because public documents cannot tie specific shipments to specific cars.
om_angle: The investigation shows that public data can reconstruct a supply path several tiers deep but cannot confirm that a specific shipment reached a specific car. That gap between plausible links and proven links is the core problem for supplier due diligence rules.
research_question: When investigations publicly link automakers to upstream environmental harm through multi-tier mineral chains, do the automakers or their cathode and cell suppliers change sourcing or traceability disclosures, and are the market effects concentrated on the brand or spread to the intermediate tiers?
data_identification: Run an event study around Oct. 16, 2026 for VW, Ford, Tesla, CATL and Huayou using CRSP or exchange data, with RepRisk or GDELT measuring media intensity. Map tiers with trade flows from UN Comtrade (Indonesian nickel intermediates to China) and company filings, and overlay mine-level tree-cover loss. A later CSDDD-type rule could serve as a follow-up shock.
keywords: supplier region risk; multi-tier traceability; nickel supply chain; deforestation

headline: EXPRESS: Mind the Cost of Disturbance: Firm-Level Supply Chain Risk and the Bank Loan Cost
summary: Using a text-based measure of firm-level supply chain risk, the paper finds that riskier supply chains lead to higher bank loan spreads. Using natural disasters as shocks, it shows the effect is causal, and stronger when lenders have less private information about the firm.

headline: Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
summary: The paper models a fresh-produce firm that uses sensors to monitor each unit's condition and sends units with shorter remaining shelf life to closer markets, and it analyzes when this monitoring actually reduces food waste.

headline: PJM ran on 66% of its generation fleet during October Maximum Generation Alerts; about a quarter of outages were unplanned
summary: During the week of Oct. 12, 2026, PJM had just over 61,000 MW of generation out (only 66% of fleet capacity available). More than two-thirds of outages were planned maintenance and about 15,000 MW were unplanned (preliminary), roughly a quarter rather than the one-third in some headlines. PJM recalled about 10,000 MW and called Demand Response on Oct. 13–14 for weather it called warm but 'not extreme.' DR has now been used on 15 days in 2025–2026 versus 8 in all of 2015–2024. PJM blames year-round data center load growing faster than supply and transmission, plus longer weather extremes that push into spring and fall maintenance seasons.
om_angle: Planned-maintenance scheduling is a classic OM problem, and data center load is flattening the seasonal demand trough it depends on. Outage coordination, recall decisions and DR use now trade reliability against winter readiness.
research_question: How does growth in year-round large-load demand change the optimal timing of generator maintenance, and has it raised shoulder-season scarcity events and prices in PJM?
data_identification: Use PJM Data Miner for hourly load, outages, emergency actions and DR events from 2015–2026. Combine with EIA-860 and EIA-923 for unit characteristics and EIA-930 for hourly demand. Exploit zone-level variation in data center load growth (e.g., Dominion zone vs. others) in a panel of zone-days to test whether shoulder-season alerts, real-time prices and maintenance deferrals rise with large-load share.
keywords: data center electricity demand; grid reliability standards; maintenance scheduling; demand response; load forecasting

headline: FMC proposes $200,000 per-voyage fee on Spanish-flagged vessels and possible limits on Spanish imports
summary: On Oct. 14 the Federal Maritime Commission proposed a $200,000 per-voyage fee on Spanish-flagged vessels and possible import restrictions on Spanish perfumery and cosmetics, oils and fats, ceramics, stone articles, and sugar and confectionery (docket FMC-2026-0463). The action follows a 2024 investigation finding Spain denied port access to U.S.-flagged ships, including two Maersk vessels carrying Maritime Security Program cargo; Spain cited EU regulations. Comments are due Dec. 14, Spain will be offered a hearing, and the docket expects restricted goods to be replaced mostly from other countries.
om_angle: This is a narrow, product-specific trade shock with a clear announcement date. It allows study of importer sourcing substitution and of carrier flag or routing responses.
research_question: Following the FMC announcement, how fast do U.S. importers of the targeted Spanish product categories shift to alternative origins, and does pre-buying occur before restrictions take effect?
data_identification: Use USITC DataWeb or Census USA Trade Online monthly imports by HS line. Compare targeted Spanish categories to untreated Spanish goods and to the same HS lines from Italy, Portugal and France in a difference-in-differences design around Oct. 14 and the final rule date. Panjiva bill-of-lading data (commercial) can add importer-level substitution, and the Federal Register docket supplies event timing.
keywords: sourcing restrictions; supplier diversification; pre-buy behavior; maritime policy

headline: Haleon adds an EU ETS carbon price to supplier bids, shifting 1–2 of every 10 deals
summary: Haleon asks most suppliers to estimate the carbon footprint of each purchase. It multiplies that figure by the EU ETS price (about €80/t CO2) and adds it to the bid, so the lowest combined total wins. The charge averages about 2% of bid value (about 10% for plastic bottles, about 1% for acetaminophen) and shifts 1–2 in 10 deals to pricier, lower-carbon bidders, per Haleon's Chris Low. Nearly a quarter of key suppliers now measure emissions directly, up from none in 2024. Haleon is piloting contracts with annual emission-reduction commitments and financial penalties, toward a 42% Scope 3 cut over 2022–2030; its latest report shows 13%.
om_angle: A shadow carbon price in scoring auctions is a concrete mechanism-design lever for Scope 3. It raises questions about supplier misreporting of footprints and the incentive to invest in measurement.
research_question: In a scoring auction that adds a carbon charge based on supplier-reported footprints, when does the buyer gain from rewarding primary measurement over industry-average estimates, and how much emission reduction does the charge buy per dollar of higher procurement cost?
data_identification: Analytical: model a scoring auction with a carbon price and private, possibly misreported, footprints. Empirical: use the CDP supply chain module, where Haleon's suppliers respond, to compare supplier measurement adoption and emissions before and after 2024 against suppliers of peer consumer-health firms. SBTi dashboard target validations can serve as a supplier-level outcome.
keywords: supplier emissions; scope 3 disclosure; internal carbon pricing; procurement auctions

headline: Patagonia folds Worn Wear resale into its main store after selling ~160,000 used items ($13M) in fiscal 2026
summary: Patagonia is closing the separate nine-year-old Worn Wear site and listing used items next to new ones on its main store, with a shared cart and the same warranty. It sold almost 160,000 verified secondhand items (about $13M) in fiscal 2026. More than 40 staff in Reno processed about 230,000 garments in 2025, and about 80% were resellable. The switch took a multiyear IT overhaul to handle unique SKUs, discontinued items and condition-based pricing that Trove previously managed.
om_angle: Mixing one-of-a-kind used inventory with new stock raises cannibalization, uncertain-supply and condition-pricing questions that closed-loop supply chain models have mostly studied in separate channels.
research_question: Does listing used items alongside new ones on a brand's main site cannibalize or complement new-product sales, and how should condition-based prices be set when returns supply is uncertain?
data_identification: Event study around the integration date using web-scraped listings and prices from Patagonia's site, comparing product categories with high versus low used availability. Brands that keep resale separate, such as Eileen Fisher Renew, serve as a comparison. Analytically, model joint pricing of new and graded used units with stochastic take-back supply.
keywords: closed-loop supply chain; recommerce; cannibalization; condition-based pricing

headline: Hormuz attacks hit a record six ships in one day; Singapore-flagged feeder GFS Pride sinks with containers aboard
summary: At least 10 vessels were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz from Oct. 11, including six on that day alone, the most in a single day since the U.S.–Iran war began in February. UKMTO logged 12 attacks Oct. 5–11, a weekly record. The 2,824-TEU feeder GFS Pride was struck Oct. 13 and sank off Oman with all 21 crew safe; the cause is disputed between a mine and projectiles or a drone. GFS Giselle and DP World Kaveri were also hit, and Maersk, ONE, PIL and OOCL had schedules on some affected ships. Kpler counted 131 transits in the week to Oct. 14 versus 176 the week before, with crude flows down to about 12.6M b/d from about 15M at end-September.
om_angle: Slot-sharing on feeder ships spreads risk to carriers whose names appear on bills of lading. War-risk insurance can be cancelled on short notice in these cases, a contractual fragility in shared transport capacity.
research_question: How do carriers adjust capacity sharing (slot charters on third-party feeders) and freight rates in response to escalating chokepoint attack intensity?
data_identification: Build a weekly panel from UKMTO incident counts and IMO casualty data as the shock measure. Outcomes are Kpler or AIS-based transit counts and Xeneta or Drewry rates on Gulf lanes (commercial; public Drewry WCI headlines as a fallback). GDELT event counts can serve as a public intensity proxy. Compare Gulf feeder services to non-Gulf services operated by the same carriers.
keywords: freight rates; chokepoint disruption; war-risk insurance; slot sharing

headline: Operations Management in the Sharing Economy: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
summary: This survey organizes OM research on the sharing economy into eight categories (ride, space, bike and vehicle sharing, group buying, crowdfunding and others). For each it outlines advances and open problems around matching, pricing and capacity.

headline: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
summary: In a field experiment with a state transportation department, adding modest friction to carpool-platform sign-up cut sign-ups 25% but increased overall usage. Selection explains only part of the effect.

headline: Pennsylvania PUC proposes curtailing new data centers before other customers during grid emergencies
summary: On Oct. 1, 2026 the Pennsylvania PUC voted 4-0 for a Tentative Order. Under it, utilities would curtail eligible new large loads, such as data centers that haven't secured enough new capacity, before other customers during PJM 'Interim Resource Adequacy Service' events, and could not classify data centers as exempt 'critical load.' Utilities would also have to keep large-load registries and set notification procedures. A PUC-commissioned study found PJM failing its reliability planning standard from 2027 to 2030, with modeled risk nearly six times the standard by 2030. Comments are due within 30 days plus 15 for replies, and CBS reports a final order is expected at the end of January.
om_angle: This turns large-load interruptibility into a regulated priority rule, which changes the expected cost of siting a data center in one PJM state versus its neighbors. It is a clean setting for studying curtailment priority, capacity procurement and facility location together.
research_question: Does a state rule placing un-backed large loads first in the curtailment queue shift data-center siting, or the speed of bring-your-own-capacity deals, away from Pennsylvania toward other PJM states?
data_identification: Treat Pennsylvania as treated and other PJM states as controls, with the Oct. 2026 Tentative Order and the expected January final order as shock dates. Measure outcomes with large-load interconnection requests and utility large-load filings in state PUC dockets, PJM load forecasts, and new-generation and co-location filings in EIA-860 and LBNL queue data. The unit of analysis is the utility zone by quarter.
keywords: interruptible load; data center electricity demand; grid reliability standards; facility siting; federal-state jurisdiction

headline: Mighty Earth report: US firms held 350+ EU meetings to delay and weaken the Deforestation Regulation
summary: The Guardian (Oct. 17, 2026) reported a Mighty Earth investigation finding that 24 US companies and trade groups held more than 350 meetings with EU officials between July 2024 and July 2026 over the EUDR: 173 with MEPs and 178 with senior Commission officials. These figures are relayed second-hand. Named players include Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz, the US Soybean Export Council and AmCham EU. After a July 2025 Trump–von der Leyen meeting, a joint statement promised the US special treatment, and the Commission called the US 'negligible risk.' The firms deny coordinating and cite implementation problems such as IT systems and unclear obligations.
om_angle: Traceability and due-diligence costs in commodity supply chains depend on how the rules end up written. Lobbying intensity and country-risk designations are measurable inputs that shape those rules.
research_question: Do commodity firms with greater exposure to EUDR-covered sourcing lobby more intensively, and did 'negligible risk' country designations shift EU sourcing of soy and wood products toward low-risk-rated origins?
data_identification: Firm-level meeting counts would come from the EU Transparency Register and Commission meeting logs. EUDR exposure could be built from commodity import shares in UN Comtrade (Panjiva bills of lading where available). A difference-in-differences design would compare EU imports by origin before and after the July 2025 US designation and the later postponement and dilution steps, whose legal status should be verified.
keywords: deforestation; multi-tier traceability; regulatory uncertainty; corporate lobbying

headline: Infineon adds Wolfspeed 200mm silicon carbide wafers in multi-year supply deal
summary: On Oct. 15, 2026 Infineon and Wolfspeed announced a multi-year agreement for Wolfspeed to supply 200mm SiC wafers. Wolfspeed calls it an expansion and extension of their existing 150mm deal, a relationship of more than 20 years, while Infineon frames it as supporting its move from 150mm to 200mm. Infineon cites its multi-supplier strategy and rising SiC demand from EVs, renewables and AI data center power systems. Value, volumes and duration were not disclosed.
om_angle: This is a long-term contract signed during a technology transition, with the buyer deliberately multi-sourcing a concentrated input. It is useful for studying how wafer-size transitions interact with supplier diversification and the risk of a supplier failing.
research_question: When a critical input undergoes a technology node transition (150mm to 200mm SiC), do buyers lengthen contracts and add suppliers, and how does supplier financial distress affect those choices?
data_identification: Collect supply-agreement disclosures from SEC EDGAR 8-Ks and 10-K material-contract exhibits, plus Compustat customer segments, to build buyer–supplier dyads. FactSet Revere is a commercial alternative. The design would compare contract terms and the number of suppliers per buyer before and after 200mm announcements across SiC buyers, conditioning on supplier distress measures from Compustat.
keywords: supplier diversification; supplier concentration; long-term supply contracts; silicon carbide

headline: India's draft National Steel Policy 2047 targets 604 MT and emphasizes circularity and secondary producers
summary: PTI reported on Oct. 17 that industry welcomed India's draft National Steel Policy 2047, released for comment. Its 2047 targets are 604 MT of crude steel (sources disagree on whether this is capacity or production), 505 MT of finished-steel demand, 302 kg per capita consumption and 45 MT of exports. The draft stresses value addition, raw-material security, decarbonisation, coated and specialty steel, and support for secondary producers. RHI Magnesita India highlighted the draft's recognition of refractory recovery.
om_angle: This is a large policy shift in the world's fastest-growing major steel market, linking circularity (secondary steel, refractory recovery) with raw-material security and decarbonisation. It is relevant to recycling capacity and secondary-material sourcing.
research_question: How do policy commitments to secondary steel producers and material recovery change the mix of primary and secondary steelmaking capacity, and India's import dependence for scrap and raw materials?
data_identification: Track India's imports of ferrous scrap, coking coal and magnesite by HS code in UN Comtrade before and after the draft and the final policy, with peer steel-producing countries as comparison. Pair this with plant-level capacity and production statistics. Note that the final policy text and timing still need to be verified.
keywords: steel decarbonization; secondary materials; raw material security; industrial policy

headline: Pentagon commits $450M to tungsten producer Elmet in exchange for preferred equity and warrants
summary: On Sept. 14, 2026 Elmet Group announced a $450M committed investment from the US Department of War to expand tungsten mining, processing and manufacturing: $200M at closing, with further drawdowns. In return the government gets redeemable preferred equity, warrants for up to 19.9% of common stock, and a board seat plus an observer. The Department also took about a 10% stake through roughly $35.6M of transactions involving Trilogy Metals and South32's Alaska projects. This is a late-September wrap; ELMT rose over 33% that week, and the deal's closing and the subsequent Trump–Xi meeting outcome are unconfirmed here.
om_angle: Governments are moving from grants and loans to equity and governance rights in mineral suppliers. That raises questions about how state ownership changes capacity investment and sourcing for concentrated inputs like tungsten.
research_question: How do markets and firms respond when the US government takes equity stakes in critical-mineral producers? Specifically, do recipients accelerate capacity investment, and do rivals' valuations move?
data_identification: Build an event study on announcement dates of government equity deals (Elmet, Trilogy and others), using 8-K exhibits from SEC EDGAR and CRSP returns for recipients and listed peers. Follow-up outcomes would be capex and capacity from Compustat and 10-Ks, and US import dependence for tungsten from USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries.
keywords: supplier concentration; capacity investment under uncertainty; government equity stakes; tungsten

headline: EXPRESS: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
summary: The paper asks why operational or disclosure improvements often don't raise market value. It models equity value as the minimum across several valuation 'lenses,' so the single weakest firm condition (for example, a governance or financing concern) binds and gets disproportionate weight.

headline: Startup forecasts 57% jump in 2026 emissions for five hyperscalers, using capex to predict emissions before disclosure
summary: Bricola Group, a startup founded by former Amazon economist Jimmy Gillan, forecasts that combined emissions of Alphabet, AWS, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle will rise 57% in 2026 to 215 million tCO2e gross. Net of renewable energy certificates and similar purchases, the forecast is 140 million tCO2e, up from 87 million in 2025; AWS and Alphabet are each expected at just over 53 million tCO2e. The model maps past capex to past emissions. Capex is reported in 10-Ks 5–9 months before sustainability reports, and the five firms' combined 2025–2026 capex is expected to exceed $1 trillion. These are first-use model estimates with no outside validation, and Alphabet, AWS and Meta rely on capex guidance rather than reported figures.
om_angle: Capex-to-emissions mapping is a forward-looking emissions estimator, and it can be tested against what firms later report. The forecast also measures how far AI capacity growth outruns corporate decarbonization, including the gap between gross and certificate-adjusted (market-based) accounting.
research_question: How well does capital expenditure predict a firm's later-reported Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, and does the predictive gap widen during capacity build-outs such as AI data centers?
data_identification: Build a firm-year panel of capex and PP&E from Compustat or SEC EDGAR 10-Ks, matched to emissions in CDP responses and sustainability reports. Estimate out-of-sample prediction errors before and after 2023, treating the AI capex surge as the shock and comparing hyperscalers with other capex-heavy firms. Compare location-based emissions with market-based (certificate-adjusted) emissions, and add facility-level power-sector context from EPA eGRID.
keywords: data center electricity demand; emissions forecasting; capital expenditure; market-based emissions accounting

headline: Experts argue better sorting and updated bottle bills could ease US aluminum shortage more cheaply than new smelters
summary: Amid a global aluminum shortage and US tariffs, Canary Media reports that millions of tons of US aluminum scrap still end up in landfills. Recycled aluminum needs only 5% of the energy of primary metal, while new or restarted smelters must compete with data centers for cheap power. SAFE's report says the US imports 84% of its primary aluminum, runs only five smelters in 2026, and faces primary demand rising from 4.4 to 5.1 million tons by 2029. Proposed fixes include Sortera's alloy-sorting plants (a $45M raise for a second site in Tennessee) and updating the 10 state bottle bills; Massachusetts' 5-cent deposit is 43 years old.
om_angle: This is a concrete primary-versus-secondary sourcing trade-off in which energy prices, tariffs and collection policy all set the economics of closed-loop supply. Sorting quality decides whether scrap becomes high-value alloy or is downcycled into low-value products.
research_question: Do states with bottle-deposit laws, and higher deposit values, achieve higher aluminum recovery and lower landfill disposal, and does that translate into more domestic secondary aluminum supply?
data_identification: Run state-level panels comparing the 10 deposit states with non-deposit states, using EPA materials and waste data, state recycling and EPR program reports, and changes in deposit law over time. Track aluminum scrap exports and imports by HS code in Census USA Trade Online to see whether higher tariffs shift scrap toward domestic remelting.
keywords: secondary materials; closed-loop supply chain; state environmental policy; deposit return systems; raw material security

headline: US reportedly weighing critical-minerals price floor with allies; reports conflict on whether it will proceed
summary: Citing Bloomberg, Stocktwits reported a multi-agency US plan for a critical-minerals price floor, to be rolled out through the Pax Silica program after a 55-country summit, with reported agreements with the EU, Japan and Mexico. MP, USAR, UAMY and TMC each rose more than 2% pre-market. On January 28, Reuters had reported the administration was stepping back from price floors because Congress had not funded them, and those stocks fell 5–10% after hours. MP Materials said its own $110/kg floor contract for light rare earths remains in force. The article is stamped March 5, 2026, so it is roughly seven months old, and the policy's current status is unverified.
om_angle: A guaranteed minimum price is a market-design intervention that shifts demand risk from producers to the government, which should change capacity investment and buyers' sourcing decisions. The back-and-forth news flow gives clean event dates for testing that.
research_question: How do announcements and reversals of price-floor support change rare-earth producers' valuations and their announced capacity investments, compared with downstream buyers'?
data_identification: Run an event study on the January 28 Reuters report and the Bloomberg price-floor report, using CRSP returns for producers (MP, USAR, UAMY, TMC, CRML) against downstream users identified through Compustat customer segments or FactSet Revere. Follow up with capex and capacity announcements in SEC 8-Ks and 10-Ks, and benchmark against USGS mineral data.
keywords: industrial policy; raw material security; capacity investment under uncertainty; price floors; regulatory uncertainty

headline: Microsoft signs 20-year, 1.1 GW deal with NiSource for Indiana data center, paying for all new infrastructure
summary: Microsoft agreed to a 20-year contract with NiSource for about 1,100 MW of generation for a northwest Indiana data center campus, starting in 2028. DCD thinks the site is likely La Porte, but this is unconfirmed. Power flows through NiSource's GenCo subsidiary under a new rate structure for very large customers. Microsoft pays for all required generation and transmission, and GenCo has contracted 600 MW of battery storage. NiSource raised its estimate of savings for existing customers from its data center contracts to about $1.75B, up from $1.4B, or up to $140 per customer per year.
om_angle: Under this 'pay your own way' structure, a dedicated generation subsidiary and the large customer carry the build-out risk. That is a contract design for allocating capacity risk between hyperscalers and regulated ratepayers, and it is likely to spread to other utilities.
research_question: Do dedicated large-load tariffs and generation-subsidiary structures like NiSource's GenCo shield residential rates from data center load growth, compared with utilities that serve data centers under standard tariffs?
data_identification: Compare utility-level residential rates and sales in EIA-861 for utilities adopting large-load tariffs versus those that have not, with adoption dates taken from state PUC dockets such as the Indiana IURC NIPSCO filings. Add generator and storage additions from EIA-860 to measure the capacity actually built per contracted MW.
keywords: data center electricity demand; long-term supply contracts; battery storage; large-load tariffs; facility siting
